questions.question: Which of the following states has launched Digital Seva Setu Programme for the rural areas in October 2020?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gujarat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Digital Seva Setu Programme** was launched by the Government of Gujarat in October 2020.
 
• This program aims to provide government services online to rural citizens through **e-gram panchayats**.
 
• Under this initiative, over 22,000 village panchayats in Gujarat were connected through an **optical fibre network**.
 
• Rural citizens can access various services such as income certificates, caste certificates, and residential proof documents via the platform.
 
• The program is part of the state’s efforts to promote **digital governance** and improve the delivery of public services in rural areas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Digital Seva Setu Programme:**

 
 
• Aims to bridge the digital divide between urban and rural areas in Gujarat.
 
• Implemented in a phased manner, with the first phase including 22 services offered online.
 
• The services are delivered through the e-Gram Vishwagram Centres in rural areas.
 
 
 
• **Optical Fibre Network:**
 
 
• The program is part of the BharatNet project, which focuses on providing high-speed internet connectivity to gram panchayats in India.
 
• Optical fibre cables enable faster and more reliable internet connectivity compared to traditional copper cables.
 
 
 
• **Digital Governance in India:**
 
 
• Digital initiatives such as Digital India aim to transform India into a digitally empowered society and knowledge economy.
 
• By providing digital access to government services, programs like Digital Seva Setu enhance transparency and accountability.
 
 
 
• **Village Panchayats:**
 
 
• Village panchayats are the grassroots level of governance in rural India under the Panchayati Raj system.
 
• They play a vital role in implementing government schemes and ensuring the welfare of rural citizens.

questions.question: Which of the following is a kharif crop?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Jute**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Jute is a **kharif crop**, typically sown during the monsoon season (June to July).
 
• It requires a warm and humid climate with temperatures ranging from **24°C to 37°C**.
 
• The crop thrives in regions with **high rainfall (120-150 cm)**, making it suitable for cultivation in areas like West Bengal, Bihar, Assam, and Odisha.
 
• Jute is primarily grown in **alluvial soil**, which retains moisture and is highly fertile.
 
• India is the world's largest producer of jute, contributing significantly to its economy and exports.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Kharif Crops**

 
 
• Kharif crops are grown during the monsoon season, which starts in June and ends in October.
 
• They require high temperatures and significant rainfall for growth.
 
• Examples include rice, maize, cotton, jute, and groundnut.
 
 
 
• **Jute Production in India**
 
 
• West Bengal is the leading producer of jute in India, accounting for approximately **80% of the total production**.
 
• It is used primarily in making gunny bags, ropes, carpets, and other coarse fabrics.
 
• Jute is often referred to as the "Golden Fiber" due to its economic importance.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between Kharif and Rabi Crops**
 
 
• Kharif crops are grown in the rainy season, while Rabi crops are grown in the winter season.
 
• Rabi crops include wheat, barley, mustard, and peas.
 
• Rabi crops require cool weather and less water compared to Kharif crops.
 
 
 
• **Environmental Importance of Jute**
 
 
• Jute is biodegradable and eco-friendly, making it a sustainable alternative to plastic.
 
• It plays an important role in soil conservation and helps prevent erosion in flood-prone areas.

questions.question: On which of the following dates is the International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies observed?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**7 September**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **International Day of Clean Air for Blue Skies** is observed annually on **September 7** to emphasize the importance of clean air and a sustainable environment.
 
• This day was established by the **United Nations General Assembly (UNGA)** during its** 74th session in December 2019**.
 
• The day aims to raise awareness about air pollution, its impacts on health, the environment, and the economy.
 
• It encourages global collaboration and action to reduce air pollution and achieve cleaner, healthier air globally.
 
• Various campaigns, events, and educational programs are organized worldwide to mark this day and promote sustainable practices.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Air Pollution:**

 
 
• Air pollution refers to the presence of harmful substances in the air, such as particulate matter (PM), carbon monoxide, sulfur dioxide, nitrogen oxides, and volatile organic compounds.
 
• It is a major environmental risk factor for various health conditions, including respiratory diseases, cardiovascular problems, and premature mortality.
 
 
 
• **Key Contributors to Air Pollution:**
 
 
• Major sources include industrial emissions, vehicle exhaust, deforestation, agricultural activities, and burning of fossil fuels.
 
• Indoor air pollution is also significant in developing countries due to the use of biomass fuels for cooking and heating.
 
 
 
• **Global Efforts to Combat Air Pollution:**
 
 
• International initiatives like the UN Environment Programme (UNEP) and the Climate and Clean Air Coalition (CCAC) work to mitigate air pollution.
 
• The adoption of sustainable practices such as renewable energy, improved waste management, and electric mobility contribute to cleaner air.
 
 
 
• **Impact of Clean Air:**
 
 
• Clean air improves public health by reducing respiratory and cardiovascular diseases.
 
• It positively impacts ecosystems, biodiversity, and agriculture, promoting sustainability.
 
• Cleaner air also boosts economic productivity by reducing healthcare costs and improving worker efficiency.

questions.question: Which of the following is a Central Sector Scheme to improve ground water management launched in 2019?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Atal Bhujal Yojana**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Atal Bhujal Yojana (ABHY)** is a Central Sector Scheme launched by the Government of India in **2019** to improve groundwater management.
 
• The scheme is implemented by the **Ministry of Jal Shakti** and focuses on areas with critical groundwater resources.
 
• It aims to involve local communities in the sustainable management of groundwater resources by adopting a **community-led approach.**
 
• The programme is being implemented in **seven states**: Gujarat, Haryana, Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Rajasthan, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
• **The World Bank** is providing financial assistance for this scheme, and it focuses on both demand-side and supply-side interventions for effective groundwater management.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Groundwater Depletion in India**

 
 
• India is the largest consumer of groundwater in the world, with nearly 89% of groundwater extracted for irrigation purposes.
 
• Overexploitation of groundwater has resulted in depleting water tables, particularly in agriculturally intensive regions.
 
 
 
• **Jal Shakti Abhiyan**
 
 
• Launched in **2019**, it is a campaign aimed at water conservation and rainwater harvesting across India.
 
• It focuses on five key aspects: water conservation, rainwater harvesting, reuse of water, watershed development, and afforestation.
 
 
 
• **National Water Mission**
 
 
• It is one of the eight missions under the National Action Plan on Climate Change (NAPCC).
 
• The mission aims to ensure the sustainable use of water resources and enhance water use efficiency by **20%**.
 
 
 
• **Integrated Watershed Management Programme (IWMP)**
 
 
• This is a centrally sponsored scheme under the Department of Land Resources, launched in **2009-10**.
 
• It aims to restore ecological balance by harnessing, conserving, and developing degraded natural resources like soil and water.

questions.question: Which among the following is one of the States/union territories that accommodates a part of Oussudu Lake Bird Sanctuary?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Puducherry**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Oussudu Lake Bird Sanctuary**, also known as **Osudu Lake**, is a prominent freshwater lake located in the union territory of **Puducherry** and partly in Tamil Nadu.
 
• The lake is designated as one of the most important wetlands in India under the Ramsar Convention for its ecological significance.
 
• It serves as a habitat for numerous migratory and resident bird species, making it a crucial site for birdwatching and biodiversity conservation.
 
• Spread across approximately **390 hectares**, the sanctuary is a popular eco-tourism destination in the region.
 
• The Puducherry government has taken initiatives to protect and preserve the lake's biodiversity through conservation measures and awareness programs.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Wetlands:**

 
 
• Wetlands are areas where water covers the soil or is present near the surface of the soil for varying periods.
 
• They are vital ecosystems that provide habitat for biodiversity, regulate water levels, and act as natural water purifiers.
 
• The Ramsar Convention recognizes wetlands of international importance for their ecological significance.
 
 
 
• **Ramsar Sites in India:**
 
 
• India has over 75 Ramsar sites recognized for their importance under the Ramsar Convention.
 
• These sites protect the biodiversity and ensure sustainable use of water resources.
 
• Examples include Chilika Lake, Sundarbans Wetland, and Sambhar Lake.
 
 
 
• **Migratory Birds:**
 
 
• Migratory birds travel across regions and countries to find suitable habitats during different seasons.
 
• Bird sanctuaries like Oussudu Lake play a key role in providing temporary shelter to these species.
 
• Conservation efforts help maintain the ecological balance and protect these species from threats.
 
 
 
• **Eco-Tourism:**
 
 
• Eco-tourism promotes travel to natural areas to conserve the environment and improve the well-being of local people.
 
• Oussudu Lake Bird Sanctuary is a prime example of eco-tourism, attracting bird watchers and nature enthusiasts.
 
• Proper management of eco-tourism sites ensures sustainable development and conservation of natural habitats.

questions.question: How many years did Constitutional Assembly approximately take to draft the Constitution?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Three**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Constituent Assembly of India was established on **9th December 1946** and began drafting the Indian Constitution.
 
• The final draft of the Constitution was adopted on **26th November 1949**, marking a period of nearly three years of deliberations.
 
• The Constitution came into effect on **26th January 1950**, celebrated annually as Republic Day.
 
• The drafting committee, chaired by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**, played a pivotal role in formulating the Constitution.
 
• Approximately **299 members** were part of the Constituent Assembly during the adoption of the Constitution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Constituent Assembly:**

 
 
• The Constituent Assembly was formed under the **Cabinet Mission Plan** in 1946.
 
• Its main purpose was to draft the Constitution of India and manage the transition of India from British rule to independence.
 
• Initially, the assembly had **389 members**, which reduced after the partition to **299 members**.
 
 
 
• **Drafting Committee:**
 
 
• The Drafting Committee was chaired by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, often referred to as the **Architect of the Indian Constitution**.
 
• It consisted of **7 members**, including notable figures like Alladi Krishnaswami Ayyar and N. Gopalaswami.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the Constitution:**
 
 
• The Indian Constitution is the **longest written Constitution** in the world.
 
• It incorporates elements from various countries such as **the parliamentary system from Britain** and the **federal structure from the USA**.
 
• It establishes India as a **sovereign, socialist, secular, and democratic republic**.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Republic Day:**
 
 
• 26th January was chosen as the date to implement the Constitution to honor the declaration of **Purna Swaraj** in 1930.
 
• India became a republic on this day, officially marking its transition to a constitutional democracy.

questions.question: Which of the following monetary policy tool is used by the Reserve Bank of India to control liquidity and inflation in the economy?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Repo Rate**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The **Repo Rate** is the rate at which the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) lends short-term funds to commercial banks in case of a liquidity shortage.
 
• By increasing the repo rate, the RBI can make borrowing costlier for banks, thereby reducing the money supply and curbing inflation.
 
• Conversely, lowering the repo rate encourages borrowing and increases liquidity in the economy, stimulating growth.
 
• The repo rate is a crucial monetary policy tool used by the RBI to maintain inflation within its target range and to ensure economic stability.
 
• As of October 2023, the RBI’s Monetary Policy Committee (MPC) reviews the repo rate every two months to ensure effective economic management.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Reverse Repo Rate:**

 
 
• This is the rate at which the RBI borrows money from commercial banks in the short term.
 
• It is used to absorb excess liquidity from the banking system.
 
 
 
• **Cash Reserve Ratio (CRR):**
 
 
• It is the percentage of a commercial bank's net demand and time liabilities (NDTL) that must be kept as reserves with the RBI.
 
• An increase in CRR reduces the funds available for lending, thereby controlling inflation.
 
 
 
• **Statutory Liquidity Ratio (SLR):**
 
 
• It is the percentage of NDTL that commercial banks must maintain in the form of liquid assets like cash, gold, or approved government securities before providing credit to customers.
 
• SLR is used to control credit expansion and manage inflation.
 
 
 
• **Monetary Policy Committee (MPC):**
 
 
• The MPC is a committee formed by the RBI to determine interest rates and monetary policy in India.
 
• The MPC meets bi-monthly to review economic conditions and decide on key policy rates like the repo rate and reverse repo rate.

questions.question: A branch of science, that deals with the sequence of all periodical events involved in a plant life cycle, that helps to understand the weather dynamics on vegetative and reproductive growth period of the crop is called ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Phenology**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Phenology is the scientific study of periodic biological events in the life cycle of plants and animals, influenced by climatic and seasonal changes.
 
• In plants, phenology focuses on events like germination, flowering, fruiting, and leaf shedding, which are critical for understanding crop productivity.
 
• It helps in predicting the impact of weather dynamics on vegetative and reproductive growth stages of crops, facilitating effective agricultural planning.
 
• Phenological studies are vital for adapting agricultural practices to climate change and ensuring food security.
 
• The knowledge derived from phenology is widely applied in fields like ecology, horticulture, and climate science.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Carpology:**

 
 
• Carpology is the branch of botany that deals with the study of fruits and seeds.
 
• It focuses on understanding the structure, development, and classification of seeds and fruits.
 
 
 
• **Petrology:**
 
 
• Petrology is the scientific study of rocks, including their origin, composition, structure, and distribution.
 
• It is a key branch of geology and helps in understanding Earth's crust and its evolution.
 
 
 
• **Palaeontology:**
 
 
• Palaeontology is the study of fossils to understand the history of life on Earth.
 
• It provides insights into the evolution and extinction of plant and animal species over geological time.
 
 
 
• **Importance of Phenological Studies:**
 
 
• Phenological data is used for forecasting agricultural yields and managing pests and diseases.
 
• It aids in designing adaptive strategies for climate-resilient agriculture.
 
• The data is also applied in biodiversity conservation by predicting the responses of species to climate change.

questions.question: In which of the following states, is the irrigation and power generation Sharda canal located?
questions.solution:

__
 
• The **Sharda Canal system**, located in **Uttar Pradesh**, is one of the largest irrigation projects in India.
 
• The canal originates from the Sharda River, a tributary of the Ghaghra River, which flows through northern India.
 
• It was constructed primarily for irrigation and power generation purposes, significantly aiding agricultural productivity in the region.
 
• The Sharda Canal system irrigates vast areas of the state, particularly in districts like Pilibhit, Shahjahanpur, and Hardoi.
 
• This canal has been pivotal in transforming Uttar Pradesh into one of the leading agricultural states in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Sharda River:**

 
 
• The Sharda River, also known as Mahakali River in Nepal, originates from the Himalayas and flows through Uttarakhand and Uttar Pradesh.
 
• The river is an important water source for irrigation and hydroelectric projects in the region.
 
 
 
• **Canal Irrigation in India:**
 
 
• Canal irrigation is one of the oldest and most widespread methods of irrigation in India.
 
• It involves diverting river water into canals to irrigate agricultural fields.
 
• India has extensive canal networks, particularly in northern states like Punjab, Haryana, and Uttar Pradesh.
 
 
 
• **Power Generation:**
 
 
• Hydroelectric power generation is a sustainable method of producing electricity using water flow.
 
• Canals like Sharda often incorporate hydroelectric projects to harness energy from flowing water.
 
 
 
• **Agriculture in Uttar Pradesh:**
 
 
• Uttar Pradesh is one of India’s largest agricultural states, producing crops such as wheat, sugarcane, rice, and pulses.
 
• Canal irrigation systems like Sharda play a critical role in ensuring water availability for farming activities.

questions.question: Surma the longest river, flows into which of the following countries that rises from northeast India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bangladesh**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Surma River originates from the Barak River in the northeastern part of India, specifically in the state of Assam.
 
• As it flows, the Surma River enters Bangladesh and merges with other rivers, contributing to the Meghna River system.
 
• The Surma River is a vital waterway in Bangladesh, supporting agriculture, fishing, and transportation in the region.
 
• It is one of the two main distributaries of the Barak River, with the other being the Kushiyara River.
 
• In Bangladesh, the Surma River flows through the Sylhet region, known for its lush greenery and tea gardens.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Barak River System:**

 
 
• The Barak River originates in the Indian state of Manipur and flows through Assam before splitting into the Surma and Kushiyara rivers.
 
• These rivers are part of the larger Meghna River system, which eventually drains into the Bay of Bengal.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Sylhet Region:**
 
 
• The Sylhet region in Bangladesh, through which the Surma River flows, is famous for its tea plantations and natural beauty.
 
• It is a critical region for Bangladesh’s economy due to its agricultural and fishery-based activities.
 
 
 
• **Meghna River System:**
 
 
• The Meghna River is one of the major river systems in Bangladesh, formed by the merging of the Surma and Kushiyara rivers.
 
• It plays a crucial role in the country’s water management and is vital for irrigation and transportation.
 
 
 
• **Transboundary Rivers:**
 
 
• Rivers like the Surma that flow across national boundaries are significant for regional cooperation and water resource management.
 
• India and Bangladesh share multiple rivers, which necessitates treaties and agreements for their sustainable management.

questions.question: Which of the following authority is responsible for the administration of the Government of India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The Cabinet Secretariat**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Cabinet Secretariat is primarily responsible for the administration of the Government of India and acts as the central coordinating agency between various ministries and departments.
 
• It is headed by the Cabinet Secretary, who is the senior-most civil servant in the Indian government and acts as the principal advisor to the Prime Minister.
 
• The Cabinet Secretariat's functions include facilitating decision-making in government and ensuring effective communication between ministries for smooth governance.
 
• It operates under the direct charge of the Prime Minister and ensures that the policies and decisions of the government are efficiently implemented.
 
• The Cabinet Secretariat plays a critical role in governance by preparing agendas for Cabinet meetings and coordinating the implementation of decisions taken by the Cabinet.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Cabinet Secretary:**

 
 
• The Cabinet Secretary is the administrative head of the Cabinet Secretariat and serves as the chief coordinator of the central government.
 
• This position is considered one of the most powerful roles in the Indian administrative hierarchy.
 
• The Cabinet Secretary is responsible for providing support to the Prime Minister and ensuring inter-ministerial coordination.
 
 
 
• **Structure of Cabinet Secretariat:**
 
 
• The Cabinet Secretariat consists of three wings: Civil, Military, and Intelligence.
 
• These wings collectively handle administrative functions, defense coordination, and intelligence-related matters.
 
 
 
• **Functions of the Cabinet Secretariat:**
 
 
• Coordination between ministries and departments for policy implementation.
 
• Preparation of Cabinet meeting agendas and minutes.
 
• Ensuring the proper execution of Cabinet decisions.
 
 
 
• **Prime Minister's Role:**
 
 
• The Prime Minister holds ultimate authority over the Cabinet Secretariat and its functioning.
 
• The Secretariat ensures the smooth functioning of the Prime Minister's Office and works to implement the government's policy decisions.

questions.question: Cham Mask dance, the famous folk dance of India is celebrated in which of the following countries?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Bhutan**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Cham Mask Dance is a traditional folk dance performed in **Buddhist countries**, including Bhutan, India, and Tibet.
 
• It is a sacred dance performed by monks in monasteries during **religious festivals** such as Tshechu in Bhutan.
 
• The Cham dance is characterized by colorful masks and elaborate costumes, symbolizing different deities and animals.
 
• Bhutan's Tshechu festival, which features Cham dances, is celebrated annually to honor Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava), a revered Buddhist figure.
 
• The dance serves both spiritual and cultural purposes, aiming to ward off evil spirits and bring blessings to the community.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Tshechu Festival:**

 
 
• A major annual religious event celebrated in Bhutan, dedicated to Guru Rinpoche.
 
• Includes performances of masked dances (Cham), traditional music, and rituals.
 
• The festival is an occasion for social gathering and spiritual purification.
 
 
 
• **Guru Rinpoche (Padmasambhava):**
 
 
• A legendary Buddhist saint who is believed to have brought Tantric Buddhism to Bhutan and Tibet.
 
• He is often depicted in Cham dances through symbolic masks and costumes.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Masks:**
 
 
• Masks used in Cham dances represent deities, animals, and mythical figures.

questions.question: The difference between total revenue and total expenditure of the government is termed as ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Fiscal Deficit**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The fiscal deficit is defined as the difference between the **total revenue and total expenditure** of the government in a given financial year.
 
• It indicates the total borrowing requirements of the government to meet its expenditure needs.
 
• The fiscal deficit is a key indicator of the **financial health and fiscal discipline** of a country.
 
• It is calculated using the formula: **Fiscal Deficit = Total Expenditure - (Revenue Receipts + Non-debt Capital Receipts)**.
 
• High fiscal deficits are often associated with **increased government borrowing**, which may lead to inflation and other macroeconomic imbalances.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Revenue Deficit:**

 
 
• It refers to the shortfall in the government's revenue receipts compared to its revenue expenditure.
 
• High revenue deficits indicate that the government is unable to meet its regular operational expenses through its earnings.
 
 
 
• **Primary Deficit:**
 
 
• It is the fiscal deficit minus interest payments on previous borrowings.
 
• This measure helps to understand the government's borrowing needs excluding interest obligations.
 
 
 
• **Budget Deficit:**
 
 
• The budget deficit is the difference between total government receipts and total government spending in a fiscal year.
 
• It is a broader term and includes revenue deficit, fiscal deficit, and primary deficit.
 
 
 
• **Implications of Fiscal Deficit:**
 
 
• Higher fiscal deficits can lead to increased borrowing, which may crowd out private investment.
 
• It can also result in inflationary pressures if the government prints money to finance the deficit.
 
• However, moderate fiscal deficits can stimulate economic growth during periods of slowdown.

questions.question: Which of the following kingdoms was annexed in 1848 by applying the Doctrine of Lapse?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Satara**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Satara** was the first kingdom annexed by the British East India Company in 1848 under the **Doctrine of Lapse**.
 
• The Doctrine of Lapse was a policy introduced by Lord Dalhousie, which allowed the British to annex Indian states where the ruler died without a male heir.
 
• The adoption of heirs was not recognized under this doctrine, leading to widespread annexation of territories.
 
• Satara was annexed following the death of its last ruler, **Chhatrapati Pratapsingh Maharaj**, who did not have a biological male heir.
 
• This policy became a significant cause of resentment among Indian rulers and was one of the factors leading to the **Revolt of 1857**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Doctrine of Lapse:**

 
 
• Introduced by Lord Dalhousie, Governor-General of India from 1848 to 1856.
 
• Allowed the British to annex states where the ruler did not have a biological male heir.
 
• Denied the customary practice of adopting heirs, which was a tradition in many Indian princely states.
 
 
 
• **Other Annexations under the Doctrine:**
 
 
• Other states annexed include **Jhansi (1853)**, **Nagpur (1854)**, and **Sambalpur (1850).**
 
• The policy led to significant unrest and opposition among Indian rulers.
 
 
 
• **Impact of the Doctrine:**
 
 
• It created a sense of discontent and mistrust among Indian rulers towards the British administration.
 
• Contributed to the causes of the **1857 Revolt**, which marked the beginning of organized resistance to British rule.
 
 
 
• **End of the Doctrine:**
 
 
• The policy was officially abandoned by the British after the **1857 Revolt**.
 
• Subsequent rulers were allowed to adopt heirs, and the princely states were given autonomy under British suzerainty.

questions.question: Under which Article of the Constitution can Parliament legislate with respect to matter on any subject enumerated in the State List for the national interest?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Article 249**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Article 249 of the Indian Constitution empowers Parliament to legislate on matters in the State List if it is deemed necessary in the national interest.
 
• For such legislation, a resolution must be passed by the Rajya Sabha by a majority of not less than two-thirds of the members present and voting.
 
• The resolution gives Parliament the authority to legislate on the specified matter for a period of one year, which may be extended by subsequent resolutions.
 
• This provision is primarily used in circumstances where uniformity of law across states is essential for national interest.
 
• Examples include situations related to national security, economic stability, or environmental concerns requiring coordinated legal measures across states.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **State List:**

 
 
• The State List is one of the three lists under the Seventh Schedule of the Indian Constitution, detailing subjects on which states can legislate.
 
• Examples of subjects include police, public health, agriculture, and local government.
 
 
 
• **Union List:**
 
 
• This list includes subjects on which only the Parliament has the exclusive power to legislate.
 
• Examples include defense, foreign affairs, and atomic energy.
 
 
 
• **Concurrent List:**
 
 
• Subjects on this list can be legislated upon by both the Parliament and state legislatures.
 
• Examples include education, forest conservation, and marriage laws.
 
 
 
• **Emergency Provisions:**
 
 
• Under Article 352 (National Emergency), Parliament can legislate on State List matters without requiring a resolution from the Rajya Sabha.
 
• This demonstrates the flexibility of the Indian Constitution in extraordinary circumstances.
 
 
 
• **Article 123:**
 
 
• This article empowers the President of India to promulgate ordinances during the recess of Parliament.
 
• These ordinances have the same force and effect as laws passed by Parliament but must be ratified within six weeks of the next session.

questions.question: The study of rocks is called ______.
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Petrology**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Petrology** is the scientific study of rocks, including their composition, texture, and formation processes.
 
• It is a branch of **geology** that focuses specifically on understanding the mineralogical and chemical makeup of rocks.
 
• Petrology is divided into three main branches: **igneous, sedimentary, and metamorphic petrology**, based on the type of rock formation.
 
• Petrologists use techniques such as **microscopic analysis**, X-ray diffraction, and geochemical analysis to study rocks.
 
• The knowledge gained from petrology is critical for understanding Earth's crust, resource exploration, and environmental studies.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mineralogy**:

 
 
• It is the study of minerals, their properties, chemical composition, and crystal structure.
 
• Mineralogy and petrology often overlap, as minerals are the building blocks of rocks.
 
 
 
• **Geomorphology**:
 
 
• It is the study of Earth's surface features and landforms, focusing on their formation and evolution.
 
• Geomorphology is closely related to geology but does not focus specifically on rocks.
 
 
 
• **Cryosphere**:
 
 
• The cryosphere refers to the frozen water part of the Earth system, including glaciers, ice caps, and sea ice.
 
• It is studied within climatology and Earth system sciences rather than petrology.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Petrology**:
 
 
• Petrology is used in resource exploration, including oil, natural gas, and mineral deposits.
 
• It helps understand geological processes such as volcanic activity, mountain formation, and plate tectonics.

questions.question: In RTGS the transactions are processed continuously on a transaction-by-transaction basis throughout the RTGS business hours. What does RTGS stands for?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Real Time Gross Settlement**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• **Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS)** is a system of electronic fund transfer where transactions are settled individually in real-time.
 
• RTGS is primarily used for high-value transactions and does not involve any physical exchange of money.
 
• In RTGS, settlements are processed on a **"gross basis"**, meaning transactions are settled individually without bundling or netting.
 
• The system operates during specified RTGS business hours and is maintained by central banks such as the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI).**
 
• RTGS ensures **instantaneous fund transfer**, making it faster than other methods like NEFT (National Electronic Funds Transfer).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Key Features of RTGS:**

 
 
• There is no upper limit for transactions processed via RTGS; however, the minimum amount is typically ₹2 lakh.
 
• RTGS transactions are irrevocable, ensuring a high level of security for participants.
 
• The system is specifically designed for large-value, time-sensitive transactions.
 
• RTGS transactions are settled directly in the books of the central bank, reducing settlement risks.
 
 
 
• **Difference Between RTGS and NEFT:**
 
 
• RTGS processes transactions individually in real-time, whereas NEFT settles transactions in batches.
 
• NEFT can handle smaller amounts, while RTGS focuses on high-value transactions (₹2 lakh and above).
 
• NEFT is available 24x7, while RTGS operates during fixed business hours as set by the central bank.
 
 
 
• **Role of RBI in RTGS:**
 
 
• The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) maintains and regulates the RTGS system in India.
 
• RBI ensures liquidity and stability in the RTGS system to facilitate smooth operation.
 
• The RTGS system is a critical component of the payment infrastructure managed by RBI.
 
 
 
• **Global Usage of RTGS:**
 
 
• RTGS systems are widely used by central banks across the world for high-value fund settlements.
 
• Examples include the Fedwire in the US and TARGET2 in the European Union.
 
• These systems help maintain financial stability by reducing systemic risks in monetary transactions.

questions.question: In which of the following years, was Lord North’s Regulating Act passed?

The correct answer is __**1773**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Regulating Act of 1773 was the first major step taken by the British Parliament to control and regulate the administration of the East India Company in India.
 
• It marked the beginning of British parliamentary control over the East India Company and its Indian territories.
 
• The Act established the position of the Governor-General of Bengal, with supervisory authority over Bombay and Madras.
 
• Lord Warren Hastings became the first Governor-General of Bengal under this Act.
 
• A Supreme Court was established in Calcutta (now Kolkata) in 1774 as part of this legislation to oversee legal matters.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **East India Company:**

 
 
• The East India Company was established in 1600 as a commercial trading body.
 
• It gradually transformed into a political and military force in India.
 
• By the mid-18th century, it controlled vast territories in India.
 
 
 
• **Governor-General of Bengal:**
 
 
• The Regulating Act centralized administration, making the Governor-General of Bengal the most powerful official.
 
• Later, this role evolved into the Governor-General of India.
 
 
 
• **Supreme Court in Calcutta:**
 
 
• The Supreme Court was established to ensure fair trials and legal enforcement.
 
• Its jurisdiction was limited to British subjects and specific legal matters.

• He disproved the phlogiston theory, an outdated concept that sought to explain combustion and chemical reactions.
 
• Lavoisier's work laid the foundation for the law of conservation of mass, which states that mass is neither created nor destroyed during chemical reactions.

• Lavoisier established that in a chemical reaction, the total mass of reactants is equal to the total mass of products.

• **Contributions to Chemical Nomenclature:**
 
 
• Lavoisier introduced a systematic approach to naming chemical compounds based on their composition and structure.
 
• His work helped standardize chemical language, enabling scientists to communicate more effectively.

questions.question: The Law of Inheritance was discovered by:
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Gregor Johann Mendel**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Gregor Johann Mendel is known as the **“Father of Genetics”** for his pioneering work on the inheritance of traits in pea plants.
 
• His experiments with **Pisum sativum (pea plants)** established the foundational principles of heredity, which are now called Mendel's Laws of Inheritance.
 
• Mendel discovered the concepts of **dominant and recessive traits**, which form the basis of modern genetics.
 
• He conducted systematic experiments from **1856 to 1863** and published his findings in 1866 in the journal “Verhandlungen des Naturforschenden Vereins Brünn.”
 
• His work remained largely unrecognized until it was rediscovered in **1900** by three scientists: Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns, and Erich von Tschermak.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Mendel’s Laws of Inheritance:**

 
 
• **Law of Segregation:** Each inherited trait is defined by a pair of alleles, and these alleles segregate during gamete formation, leaving each gamete with one allele.
 
• **Law of Independent Assortment:** Traits are inherited independently of one another if they are on different chromosomes.
 
• **Law of Dominance:** Dominant alleles mask the expression of recessive alleles in heterozygous individuals.
 
 
 
• **Significance of Mendel’s Work:**
 
 
• Mendel’s research laid the foundation for the field of genetics, including understanding hereditary diseases and genetic engineering.
 
• His work is integral to modern biology, influencing areas such as molecular biology, genomics, and evolutionary studies.
 
 
 
• **Terminologies in Genetics:**
 
 
• **Gene:** The basic unit of heredity that carries instructions for traits.
 
• **Allele:** Different versions of a gene that determine specific traits.
 
• **Genotype:** The genetic makeup of an organism.
 
• **Phenotype:** The observable traits expressed by an organism.
 
 
 
• **Rediscovery of Mendel’s Work:**
 
 
• Mendel’s findings were largely ignored during his lifetime but gained recognition in the early 20th century.
 
• The rediscovery of his work led to the development of modern genetics as a scientific discipline.

__
 
• **Graphite** is an allotrope of carbon and is the only non-metal that conducts electricity.
 
• It conducts electricity due to the presence of **delocalized electrons** that are free to move within its layers.
 
• The layered structure of graphite allows electrons to flow along its planes, making it a good conductor.
 
• Graphite is widely used in applications such as **electrodes, batteries, and lubricants** due to its electrical conductivity and other properties.
 
• Unlike other non-metals, graphite's unique crystalline arrangement contributes to its electrical conductivity.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Allotropes of Carbon**

 
 
• Carbon exists in several allotropic forms, such as graphite, diamond, and fullerene.
 
• Graphite is soft and slippery, whereas diamond is the hardest known natural substance.
 
• Fullerenes are spherical or tubular molecules made entirely of carbon, commonly referred to as "buckyballs" or "buckytubes."
 
 
 
• **Electrical Conductivity in Non-Metals**
 
 
• Most non-metals are insulators; however, graphite is an exception due to its free-moving electrons.
 
• Other non-metals, like iodine and bromine, do not conduct electricity effectively.
 
 
 
• **Structure of Graphite**
 
 
• Graphite has a layered structure, with each layer consisting of hexagonal arrangements of carbon atoms.
 
• The layers are held together by weak van der Waals forces, allowing them to slide over each other.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Graphite**
 
 
• Graphite is used in pencils, lubricants, and as a moderator in nuclear reactors.

questions.question: In which of the following years, was the Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act enacted in India?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**1985**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act (NDPS Act) was enacted in India in **1985**.
 
• The act aims to curb drug trafficking and drug abuse by implementing stringent regulations on the manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, and transport of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances.
 
• It provides for the **regulation and control of operations relating to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances** and prohibits their production, trade, use, and possession unless authorized.
 
• The NDPS Act prescribes **severe penalties for drug-related offenses**, including imprisonment, fines, and confiscation of property.
 
• The act has been amended multiple times, with major amendments introduced in **1988, 2001, and 2014** to improve its effectiveness and address emerging challenges.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Narcotic Drugs:**

 
 
• These are substances that induce sleep or reduce pain and are commonly used in medical treatments.
 
• Examples include morphine, heroin, and codeine.
 
 
 
• **Psychotropic Substances:**
 
 
• These are chemical substances that affect the mental state of an individual.
 
• They include drugs like LSD, MDMA, and amphetamines.
 
 
 
• **Key Features of the NDPS Act:**
 
 
• The act distinguishes between drug users/addicts and drug traffickers, aiming to provide rehabilitation for users while penalizing traffickers.
 
• Special provisions are in place for the forfeiture of property derived from drug trafficking activities.
 
 
 
• **Role of Enforcement Agencies:**
 
 
• The Narcotics Control Bureau (NCB) is the apex body under the NDPS Act responsible for enforcing anti-drug laws in India.
 
• State police and other agencies also play a critical role in the implementation of the act.
 
 
 
• **International Obligations:**
 
 
• The NDPS Act aligns with international conventions such as the **Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs (1961)**, the **Convention on Psychotropic Substances (1971)**, and the **UN Convention Against Illicit Traffic in Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances (1988)**.

questions.question: Who is the Chief Election Commissioner of India as of September 2020?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Sunil Arora**__.

__
 
• Sunil Arora served as the 23rd Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) of India from December 2, 2018, to April 12, 2021.
 
• He succeeded O.P. Rawat as the Chief Election Commissioner and was preceded by Sushil Chandra.
 
• Sunil Arora oversaw key elections during his tenure, including the 2019 Lok Sabha elections, which were one of the largest democratic exercises globally.
 
• Prior to his role as CEC, Sunil Arora served as a senior bureaucrat in the Indian Administrative Service, holding important positions such as Secretary, Ministry of Information and Broadcasting, and Secretary, Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship.
 
• He was known for implementing several reforms aimed at enhancing the transparency and efficiency of the electoral process in India.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Chief Election Commissioner of India:**

 
 
• The Chief Election Commissioner (CEC) is the head of the Election Commission of India, responsible for conducting free and fair elections in the country.
 
• The CEC is appointed by the President of India and serves for a tenure of six years or until reaching the age of 65 years, whichever is earlier.
 
• The Election Commission of India is a constitutional authority established under Article 324 of the Indian Constitution.
 
 
 
• **Role of the Election Commission:**
 
 
• The Election Commission is tasked with the responsibility of supervising, directing, and controlling elections to the Parliament, State Legislatures, and the offices of President and Vice President of India.
 
• It ensures free and fair elections by implementing the Model Code of Conduct and other electoral regulations.
 
 
 
• **Election Commission Reforms:**
 
 
• Under Sunil Arora's tenure, the Election Commission introduced measures such as the use of Voter Verifiable Paper Audit Trail (VVPAT) machines to ensure transparency.
 
• Awareness campaigns like 'Systematic Voters' Education and Electoral Participation' (SVEEP) were emphasized to increase voter participation.
 
• Strict adherence to the Model Code of Conduct was enforced during elections.
 
 
 
• **Historical Context:**
 
 
• The Election Commission of India was established on January 25, 1950.
 
• Initially, it was a single-member body, but since 1993, it has functioned as a three-member body with one Chief Election Commissioner and two Election Commissioners.

questions.question: Who among the following emperors had originally built the famous Buddhist Sanchi Stupa
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Ashoka**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• The Sanchi Stupa was originally commissioned and constructed by Emperor Ashoka in the 3rd century BCE during the Maurya dynasty.
 
• It is one of the oldest stone structures in India and a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
 
• Ashoka embraced Buddhism after the Kalinga war and promoted Buddhist architecture and teachings extensively.
 
• The stupa was built to house relics of the Buddha and to serve as a center for meditation and worship.
 
• The structure was later expanded and renovated by subsequent rulers, including the Shungas and Guptas.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Buddhist Stupas**

 
 
• A stupa is a dome-shaped structure that serves as a Buddhist shrine.
 
• It is believed to symbolize the Buddha's enlightened mind and is a sacred space for followers to practice meditation and pay homage.
 
 
 
• **Architectural Features of Sanchi Stupa**
 
 
• The central structure is a hemispherical dome built on a raised platform.
 
• It is surrounded by a stone railing and features four intricately carved gateways, known as toranas, depicting scenes from the life of Buddha.
 
 
 
• **Ashoka's Contribution to Buddhism**
 
 
• Ashoka played a pivotal role in the spread of Buddhism in India and abroad.
 
• He erected numerous stupas and pillars inscribed with Buddhist teachings throughout his empire.
 
 
 
• **UNESCO World Heritage Status**
 
 
• The Sanchi Stupa was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1989.
 
• It is considered a masterpiece of Buddhist art and architecture, attracting visitors and scholars worldwide.

questions.question: To expand which service in the international market, has the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI) launched its international subsidiary NPCI International?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**UPI**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] __Key Points__

__
 
• Unified Payments Interface (UPI) is a real-time payment system developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).
 
• NPCI launched its international subsidiary, NPCI International Payments Limited (NIPL), to expand UPI services globally.
 
• UPI is widely recognized for its ease of use, enabling instant money transfers using mobile numbers or virtual payment addresses.
 
• Countries like UAE, Singapore, and Bhutan have already adopted or are in the process of integrating UPI for their payment systems.
 
• NIPL is working to partner with financial institutions and governments worldwide to promote UPI as a global payment solution.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Unified Payments Interface (UPI):**

 
 
• Launched in April 2016, UPI revolutionized digital payments in India.
 
• It allows customers to link multiple bank accounts in a single application for seamless money transfers.
 
• UPI transactions are secured using two-factor authentication, including a mobile number and MPIN.
 
• UPI has contributed significantly to India’s transition to a cashless economy.
 
 
 
• **National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI):**
 
 
• NPCI is an umbrella organization for operating retail payments and settlement systems in India.
 
• It was established in 2008 with the support of the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) and the Indian Banks' Association (IBA).
 
• NPCI manages key payment systems like UPI, RuPay, Bharat BillPay, and Immediate Payment Service (IMPS).
 
 
 
• **Global Expansion of UPI:**
 
 
• NIPL aims to enable UPI integration in international payment systems.
 
• Partnerships with global entities such as Mashreq Bank in UAE and Liquid Group in Singapore demonstrate UPI’s international appeal.
 
• UPI has the potential to reduce dependency on cash and streamline cross-border transactions.
 
 
 
• **Benefits of UPI:**
 
 
• UPI offers instant, secure, and cost-effective money transfers, eliminating the need for traditional banking channels.
 
• It supports features like peer-to-peer payments, bill payments, and QR code-based transactions.
 
• UPI has become one of the most popular payment systems, processing billions of transactions monthly.

questions.question: Amer Fort, one of the finest examples of architecture, is situated in which of the following states?
questions.solution:

__
 
• **Amer Fort** is located near Jaipur, the capital city of Rajasthan, India.
 
• The fort was built in the late 16th century by **Raja Man Singh I**, a trusted general of Mughal Emperor Akbar.
 
• It is known for its stunning blend of **Rajput and Mughal architectural styles**.
 
• The fort is constructed using **red sandstone and marble**, adding to its grandeur and historical significance.
 
• Amer Fort is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site **“Hill Forts of Rajasthan”**, recognized in 2013.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Amber Palace:** Amer Fort is also known as Amber Palace, named after the town of Amber.
 
• The fort is famous for its **Sheesh Mahal** (Mirror Palace), where walls and ceilings are adorned with intricate mirror work.
 
• The fort overlooks **Maota Lake**, which served as the primary water source for the palace.
 
• The fort has a series of gates, courtyards, and halls, including **Diwan-i-Aam** (Hall of Public Audience) and **Diwan-i-Khas** (Hall of Private Audience).
 
• The fort is a popular tourist destination and showcases the rich history and culture of Rajasthan.
